code.title: Pass-by-value: changing the object vs re-assigning the parameter
code.python:
# The function receives a COPY of the reference; both copies point to one list.
def mutate(a):
    a[0] = 99            # writes into the shared list: the caller sees it


def reassign(a):
    a = [7, 7, 7]        # only the local name now points somewhere else


def show(a):
    return " ".join(str(x) for x in a)


arr = [1, 2, 3]
print("start:          " + show(arr))
mutate(arr)
print("after mutate:   " + show(arr))
reassign(arr)            # has no effect on arr
print("after reassign: " + show(arr))
# Time O(1), extra space O(1).

followUps:
Put both values into one object and return that object, because a method can hand back only one thing. The usual choices are a small array, a tiny class or record, or a list.

Example: to return the smallest and largest of [4, 9, 2], return new int[]{2, 9} and read res[0] and res[1].

static int[] minMax(int[] a) {
  int lo = a[0], hi = a[0];
  for (int x : a) { lo = Math.min(lo, x); hi = Math.max(hi, x); }
  return new int[]{lo, hi};
}

A second way is to pass in a mutable holder (an int[1] or an object with fields) and let the method fill it. That works because the method can change the object it was given, even though it cannot change the caller's variable. Cost: O(1) extra space for the small result object.

A method can never change the text of a String you pass in, so the caller's String always looks the same after the call. The method still receives a copy of the reference, but a String has no method that edits it, so there is nothing to mutate.

Example: inside void add(String s) { s = s + "!"; } the + builds a brand-new String "hi!" and points the local s at it. The caller's variable still points at "hi".

So to "change" a String you must return the new one and assign it: name = add(name);. If a method needs to build text in place, pass a StringBuilder instead, which is mutable. Each new String costs O(L) time and space for its L characters.

code.title: Stack frames for calls, heap for objects that outlive the call
code.python:
# Each call adds one frame to the stack; the frame is removed on return.
def count_frames(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    return 1 + count_frames(n - 1)


# The list is created on the heap, so it survives after this function returns.
def make_array():
    local = [10, 20, 30]   # 'local' (a reference) lives in the frame
    return local           # the frame goes away, the list does not


depth = 500                # kept below Python's default recursion limit of 1000
print("recursion of depth " + str(depth) + " used " + str(count_frames(depth)) + " stack frames")
arr = make_array()
total = 0
for x in arr:
    total += x
print("array made inside makeArray is still usable: " + " ".join(str(x) for x in arr))
print("sum = " + str(total))
# Time O(depth), stack space O(depth), heap space O(1).

followUps:
The variable lives on the stack and the array itself lives on the heap. The variable is only a reference (an address, 4 or 8 bytes) stored in the method's frame; the actual numbers are in an array object created by new.

Example: int[] a = new int[1000]; puts about 4000 bytes of data plus a 16-byte header on the heap, and one small reference called a in the frame.

When the method returns, the frame is popped and a disappears. The array stays alive only if something else still points to it (you returned it, or stored it in a field). Otherwise it becomes garbage and the collector frees it later. This is why a method can safely return an array it created.

Escape analysis is a check the JIT compiler does to see whether an object can ever be seen outside the method that created it. If the object never "escapes" (it is not returned, not stored in a field, not passed to unknown code), the JVM does not need a real heap object for it.

Example: in Point p = new Point(3, 4); return p.x + p.y; the point is used only here, so the JIT can keep 3 and 4 as two plain local values (called scalar replacement) and create no object at all. It can also drop locks on objects that only one thread can reach.

The result is less garbage and faster code, with no change in behaviour. You cannot switch it on per object or rely on it in an interview solution; it is an optimisation the JVM applies when it can prove it is safe.

code.title: Fast input and output: read tokens from a buffer, print once at the end
code.python:
import io
import sys

# In a real judge this would be sys.stdin.
source = io.StringIO("5\n3 1 4 1 5\n")
# Read everything in one go and split into tokens: much faster than input() per line.
tokens = source.read().split()
pos = 0
n = int(tokens[pos])
pos += 1
out = []                       # collect all output here
out.append("n = " + str(n))
total = 0
for _ in range(n):
    x = int(tokens[pos])
    pos += 1
    total += x
    out.append("read " + str(x) + ", running sum " + str(total))
# One write instead of n separate print calls.
sys.stdout.write("\n".join(out) + "\n")
# Time O(n), space O(n) for the tokens and the buffered output.

followUps:
Some or all of your output never appears, so the judge marks the answer wrong even though the logic is right. A PrintWriter keeps text in a memory buffer (8192 characters by default) and sends it on only when the buffer fills, or when you call flush() or close().

Example: you print 100 short lines (about 600 characters) and the program ends. Nothing reached the 8192 limit, so the screen shows nothing. With 3000 lines you would see the first part and lose the tail, which is even more confusing.

Fix: call out.flush() (or out.close()) as the last line of main, or create the writer in a try-with-resources block so it closes itself. Do not flush inside the loop, because that throws away the speed you gained from buffering.

nextInt() reads the number but leaves the Enter key (the newline) behind, so the next nextLine() returns an empty string instead of your text.

Example input:

3
hello

nextInt() returns 3 and stops just before the newline. nextLine() then reads "everything up to the end of the current line", which is nothing, so it returns "". The word hello is still waiting.

Fixes: call one extra sc.nextLine() after nextInt() to throw away the rest of that line, or read every line with nextLine() and convert with Integer.parseInt(line.trim()). The same trap exists when mixing cin >> n with getline in C++.

code.title: int vs long: the same multiplication in 32 bits and in 64 bits
code.python:
# Python ints never overflow, so this helper shows what a 32-bit int would hold.
def to_int32(x):
    return (x + 2**31) % 2**32 - 2**31


a, b = 100000, 100000
print("a = " + str(a) + ", b = " + str(b))

wrong = to_int32(a * b)        # 10^10 does not fit in 32 bits: it wraps around
right = a * b                  # the true value (what a 64-bit long holds)
print("32-bit product: " + str(wrong))
print("64-bit product: " + str(right))

max_int = 2**31 - 1            # 2147483647
nxt = to_int32(max_int + 1)    # wraps to the smallest int, no error is raised
print(str(max_int) + " + 1 in 32 bits: " + str(nxt))

# Rule: work out the largest intermediate value, then pick the type.
pairs = 100000 * 99999 // 2
print("pairs among 100000 items: " + str(pairs))
# Time O(1), space O(1).

followUps:
It evaluates to -2147483648, which is Integer.MIN_VALUE. Java does not raise an error; the value silently wraps around from the largest int to the smallest.

Why: an int is 32 bits in two's complement. The largest value is 0111…1 (31 ones). Adding 1 carries into the top bit and gives 1000…0, and a leading 1 means negative, so the pattern reads as −231.

Think of a car odometer rolling over from 999999 to 000000. This is why a running sum can suddenly turn negative. If you want an error instead of a wrap, use Math.addExact(a, b), which throws ArithmeticException. C# behaves the same by default; in C and C++ signed overflow is undefined behaviour, which is worse.

Check before you do the operation, by comparing against the limit with the operation turned around.

  • Add, b > 0: overflow if a > MAX - b.
  • Add, b < 0: overflow if a < MIN - b.
  • Multiply two positives: overflow if a > MAX / b.
if (b > 0 && a > Integer.MAX_VALUE - b) overflow();
if (b < 0 && a < Integer.MIN_VALUE - b) overflow();
int sum = a + b;   // now safe

Example: a = 2000000000, b = 200000000. MAX − b = 1947483647, and a is larger, so the sum would overflow. The check itself never overflows because MAX - b stays in range. In Java you can also call Math.addExact or Math.multiplyExact, which throw on overflow. All of these are O(1).

code.title: Integer cache: == compares objects, equals compares values

followUps:
Yes, but only the upper bound, and only with a JVM start-up option. Running Java with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=1000 makes Integer.valueOf cache every value from −128 up to 1000. The lower bound of −128 is fixed and cannot be changed.

Example: with that flag, Integer a = 1000, b = 1000; a == b prints true; without it, the same line prints false.

That is exactly why you must never depend on it. The same source code gives different answers on different machines, and on an online judge you do not control the JVM options. The language only promises the range −128 to 127. The safe habit stays the same: compare boxed numbers with .equals or unbox them to int first.

Because every key and every value in a HashMap<Integer, Integer> is a separate object, not a plain 4-byte number. Each get or put may create new Integer objects, and each lookup has to follow pointers around memory.

Rough numbers for 106 entries: an int[] needs 4 MB. The map needs one entry node (about 32 bytes) plus up to two Integer objects (16 bytes each) per entry, plus the bucket table, so roughly 50 to 70 MB. That is more than ten times the memory, plus extra work for the garbage collector and many cache misses.

Fixes: if keys fall in a small range (say 0 to 106), count with an int[] instead. Otherwise sort and scan, or use merge so each update does one lookup instead of a get followed by a put.

code.title: String building: characters copied by repeated += versus a builder
code.python:
n = 1000
print("appends: " + str(n))

# Slow way: every += makes a new string and copies all old characters.
s = ""
copied = 0
for _ in range(n):
    s += "x"
    copied += len(s)       # characters written to build this new string
print("characters copied with s += x: " + str(copied))

# Fast way: collect the pieces in a list and join them once at the end.
parts = []
written = 0
for _ in range(n):
    parts.append("x")
    written += 1           # one character per append
built = "".join(parts)
print("characters written with a builder: " + str(written))
print("both strings are equal: " + ("yes" if s == built else "no"))
# += loop: O(n^2) time in the worst case. Join: O(n) time. Both O(n) space.

followUps:
They do the same job with the same methods; the only difference is that StringBuffer is thread-safe and StringBuilder is not. Every StringBuffer method is synchronized, meaning it takes a lock so two threads cannot change the buffer at the same moment.

That lock costs a little time on every call and is wasted when only one thread uses the object, which is the normal case in an interview solution. So use StringBuilder by default. Example: building a 106-character answer does 106 appends, and each one would lock and unlock for no benefit with StringBuffer.

Choose StringBuffer only when several threads really do append to the same buffer. Both give amortised O(1) per append and O(N) total. StringBuffer is the older class (Java 1.0); StringBuilder was added in Java 5 as the faster replacement.

It is O(N2) in total. Inserting at index 0 has to shift every character already in the builder one place to the right to make room, so the k-th insert moves k − 1 characters.

Adding that up: 0 + 1 + 2 + … + (N − 1) = N(N − 1)/2. For N = 5 that is 10 moves; for N = 105 it is about 5 × 109 moves, which is far too slow.

Fix: append at the end (amortised O(1) each) and call reverse() once when you are done, which is O(N) overall.

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (char c : chars) sb.append(c);   // O(1) each
sb.reverse();                        // O(N) once

If you need to add at both ends, use an ArrayDeque<Character>. Space is O(N) either way.

code.title: Turning a constraint into a step budget: which complexity fits N = 100000
code.python:
BUDGET = 100_000_000          # about 10^8 simple steps per second


# Prints how many steps a complexity needs and whether that fits the budget.
def report(name, steps):
    verdict = "fits" if steps <= BUDGET else "too slow"
    print(name + " needs " + str(steps) + " steps: " + verdict)


n = 100000
print("N = " + str(n) + ", budget = " + str(BUDGET) + " steps per second")

# log2(N) rounded up: how many times you can halve N.
log = 0
while (1 << log) < n:
    log += 1

report("O(N)", n)
report("O(N log N)", n * log)
report("O(N^2)", n * n)       # 10^10: needs a 64-bit type in Java, C++ and C#
# Time O(log N), space O(1).

followUps:
With N ≤ 20 the setter is telling you an exponential solution is expected, so you can try every subset. There are only 220 = 1,048,576 subsets, and even doing N work per subset is about 2 × 107 steps, well inside one second.

So the toolbox changes from sorting and hashing to: bitmask enumeration (each number from 0 to 2N − 1 is one subset), backtracking, and bitmask DP with states like dp[mask] or dp[mask][last] (N × 2N states, about 2 × 107; with N transitions each, about 4 × 108, which is borderline).

What still does not fit is trying every order: 20! is about 2.4 × 1018. Trying all orders only works up to N of about 10 or 11 (10! = 3,628,800). A greedy or polynomial idea is usually wrong here, because if one existed the limit would not be so small.

It means you can treat all test cases together as one input of size 2 × 105, so an O(N) or O(N log N) solution per test is fine in total, even with 104 tests.

The trap is any work per test that does not depend on that test's N. Example: allocating or clearing a new int[1000001] inside every test. With 104 tests that is 1010 writes and a time-out, although the real data is tiny.

What to do:

  • Size arrays by the current N, or allocate once and reset only the cells you touched.
  • Clear maps and lists at the start of each test, so no data leaks from the previous one.
  • Do precomputation that all tests share (sieve, factorials) once, before the loop.

Note that O(N2) per test is still too slow: one test may have N = 2 × 105 on its own.

code.title: Brute force first, then optimise: largest sum of K consecutive elements
code.python:
# Brute force: for every start, add up the next k values. O(N*K).
def brute(a, k):
    best = None
    for i in range(len(a) - k + 1):
        total = 0
        for j in range(i, i + k):
            total += a[j]
        if best is None or total > best:
            best = total
    return best


# Optimised: the next window is the old one plus one value, minus one value. O(N).
def sliding(a, k):
    total = sum(a[:k])
    best = total
    for i in range(k, len(a)):
        total += a[i] - a[i - k]    # slide: add the new value, drop the oldest
        best = max(best, total)
    return best


a = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]
k = 3
print("array: " + " ".join(str(x) for x in a) + ", k = " + str(k))
print("brute force, O(N*K): " + str(brute(a, k)))
print("sliding window, O(N): " + str(sliding(a, k)))
# Both use O(1) extra space; the brute force is the test oracle for the fast one.

followUps:
The brute force is the final answer when it already fits the limits, or when nothing faster can exist. Check by putting the largest N into its complexity and comparing with about 108 steps per second.

  • Small constraints. N ≤ 100 with an O(N3) triple loop is 106 steps. N ≤ 10 with all orderings is 10! = 3,628,800. Both are fine as they are.
  • The output is that big anyway. "Print all subsets" must produce 2N answers, so no method can beat O(2N).
  • No better algorithm is known. Some problems (for example exact travelling salesman) have no known polynomial solution, and the small limit reflects that.

In those cases say so out loud: state the complexity, show it fits, and spend the saved time on clean code and edge cases instead of a cleverer method that adds risk.

Run the fast solution and a slow, obviously correct one on thousands of small random inputs and stop at the first input where they disagree.

  1. Keep the brute force as a separate function.
  2. Write a generator with a fixed seed: N from 1 to 8, values from −10 to 10.
  3. Loop, compare, and print the input on a mismatch.
Random rnd = new Random(1);
for (int t = 0; t < 10000; t++) {
  int[] a = gen(rnd);
  if (fast(a) != brute(a))
    { System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a)); break; }
}

Small inputs fail often and are easy to trace by hand: a failing case such as [-4, -2] immediately suggests "all negatives". The fixed seed means the same failure comes back after each fix attempt. Cost: 104 tests × tiny N runs in well under a second.

code.title: Stress test: random small inputs, brute force versus a correct and a buggy fast solution
code.python:
seed = 1


# Tiny random generator with a fixed seed, so every run gives the same tests.
def next_rand():
    global seed
    seed = (seed * 75 + 74) % 65537
    return seed


# Obviously correct: try every subarray. O(N^2).
def brute(a):
    best = a[0]
    for i in range(len(a)):
        total = 0
        for j in range(i, len(a)):
            total += a[j]
            best = max(best, total)
    return best


# Kadane, O(N). The buggy version starts best at 0, which is wrong for all-negative input.
def fast(a, buggy):
    best = 0 if buggy else a[0]
    cur = 0
    for x in a:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best


def stress(name, buggy):
    global seed
    seed = 1
    for t in range(1, 1001):
        n = 1 + next_rand() % 6                             # small sizes: 1..6
        a = [next_rand() % 21 - 10 for _ in range(n)]       # small values: -10..10
        b, f = brute(a), fast(a, buggy)
        if b != f:                                          # stop at the first mismatch
            shown = " ".join(str(x) for x in a)
            print(name + ": mismatch on test " + str(t) + ", input [" + shown + "], brute = " + str(b) + ", fast = " + str(f))
            return
    print(name + ": all 1000 tests passed")


print("problem: largest sum of a non-empty subarray")
stress("correct Kadane", False)
stress("buggy Kadane", True)
# Time O(tests * N^2) for the brute force, space O(N).

followUps:
Small values make the tricky situations happen often: equal elements, zeros, ties and sign changes. Those are where most bugs hide, and huge random numbers almost never produce them.

Numbers: pick 8 values from −10 to 10 (21 choices) and a repeated value is nearly certain, about 78% of the time. Pick 8 values from 1 to 109 and the chance of any repeat is about 3 in 100 million, so a bug in duplicate handling (< where <= was needed) would never show up.

The second reason is that a small failing case can be traced by hand. [-4, -2] tells you the story at once; six ten-digit numbers do not.

Large values test a different thing, overflow, so check that separately with one or two hand-made cases at the limits, such as all values equal to 109 with the largest N.

You test speed by generating the largest allowed input, in the shapes most likely to be slow, and timing the solution. No brute force is needed, because you are measuring time and not checking the answer.

  1. Set N to the maximum (say 2 × 105) and values to their limits.
  2. Try worst-case shapes, not only random data: already sorted, reverse sorted, all equal, a tree that is one long chain, a string of one repeated letter.
  3. Time it and compare with the limit.
long t0 = System.nanoTime();
solve(bigInput);
long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000;
System.out.println(ms + " ms");

Random data often hides the slow case: a naive quicksort is fast on random input and O(N2) on sorted input. Leave a margin, because the judge may be slower than your machine; aim for under half the limit. The same run also reveals stack overflow and memory problems.

code.title: Stable sorting: ties keep their original order
code.python:
names = ["Asha", "Ben", "Cara", "Dev", "Eli"]
scores = [90, 75, 90, 75, 60]
order = list(range(len(names)))          # positions to sort


def show(idx):
    return " ".join(names[i] + ":" + str(scores[i]) for i in idx)


print("input: " + show(order))

# sorted() uses TimSort, which is stable.
# The key is the negated score, so higher scores come first.
order = sorted(order, key=lambda i: -scores[i])

# Asha stays before Cara, and Ben before Dev: equal scores keep input order.
print("by score, high first: " + show(order))
# Time O(N log N), space O(N).

followUps:
Because the subtraction can overflow and give a result with the wrong sign, so the sort is told that a big number is smaller than a small one.

Example: a = 2,000,000,000 and b = −2,000,000,000. The true difference is 4,000,000,000, which does not fit in an int (maximum 2,147,483,647). It wraps to −294,967,296. A negative result means "a comes before b", so the sort places 2 billion before −2 billion in ascending order.

The output is then silently wrong, and with inconsistent answers TimSort can even throw "Comparison method violates its general contract".

Fix: use Integer.compare(a, b), or Comparator.comparingInt(...), which compare with < and > and never subtract. a - b is only safe when you know both values are small, for example both between 0 and 109.

A stable sort keeps items that compare as equal in the same order they had in the input. An unstable sort may swap them.

Example: sort (Ben, 75), (Asha, 90), (Dev, 75) by score. A stable sort always gives Ben, Dev, Asha: Ben stays ahead of Dev because he came first. An unstable sort might give Dev, Ben, Asha.

You need it when:

  • You sort by two keys in two passes: sort by name first, then stable-sort by score, and names stay ordered inside each score.
  • Ties must respect arrival order, for example "earlier request wins".
  • You build radix sort, which is only correct if each digit pass is stable.

It does not matter for plain numbers, since two equal ints cannot be told apart. In Java, object sorts are stable and primitive sorts are not. In C++ use stable_sort; in C# use OrderBy.

code.title: Deep recursion replaced by an explicit stack on a chain of 1,000,000 nodes
code.python:
# child[v] is the only child of node v, or -1 for the last node (a path-shaped tree).
def build_chain(n):
    return [v + 1 if v + 1 < n else -1 for v in range(n)]


# Recursive depth: one stack frame per node. Fine for 500, fails for 1,000,000.
def depth_recursive(child, v):
    if v == -1:
        return 0
    return 1 + depth_recursive(child, child[v])


# Same walk with our own stack kept on the heap, so depth is limited only by memory.
def depth_iterative(child):
    depth = [0] * len(child)
    stack = [0]
    depth[0] = 1
    best = 0
    while stack:
        v = stack.pop()                    # pop
        best = max(best, depth[v])
        c = child[v]
        if c != -1:
            depth[c] = depth[v] + 1
            stack.append(c)                # push the child
    return best


small = build_chain(500)
print("recursive, chain of 500 nodes: depth " + str(depth_recursive(small, 0)))
print("explicit stack, chain of 500 nodes: depth " + str(depth_iterative(small)))
big = build_chain(1000000)
print("explicit stack, chain of 1000000 nodes: depth " + str(depth_iterative(big)))
# Time O(N), space O(N) on the heap instead of the call stack.

followUps:
Keep your own stack of nodes: go left as far as you can while pushing, then pop one node, visit it, and move to its right child.

Deque<Node> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
Node cur = root;
while (cur != null || !st.isEmpty()) {
  while (cur != null) { st.push(cur); cur = cur.left; }
  cur = st.pop(); visit(cur); cur = cur.right;
}

The stack holds exactly the nodes whose left side is being explored, which is what the call stack held in the recursive version.

Example: root 2 with left child 1 and right child 3. Push 2, push 1; pop 1 and visit it (no right child); pop 2 and visit it, move to 3; push 3, pop and visit it. Output: 1 2 3.

Time O(N), since each node is pushed and popped once. Space O(H) for a tree of height H, which is O(N) for a chain but now on the heap, so it cannot overflow the call stack.

Usually not, because -Xss is a command-line option for the JVM and on a judge you do not write the command line; you only submit source code. Some judges do start Java with a larger stack themselves, but you cannot count on it or change it.

What you can control from inside your code is the stack size of a thread you create yourself:

public static void main(String[] a) throws Exception {
  Thread t = new Thread(null, Main::solve, "big", 1 << 26);
  t.start();
  t.join();
}

The last argument asks for 226 bytes, which is 64 MB, enough for recursion around 105 to 106 deep depending on frame size. The JVM treats that number as a hint, and the memory counts toward the judge's memory limit. An explicit stack is still the safest fix because it works everywhere.

code.title: Shallow copy shares the rows, deep copy clones each row
code.python:
def show(g):
    return " | ".join(" ".join(str(x) for x in row) for row in g)


grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
print("grid at start: " + show(grid))

# Shallow: a new outer list, but it holds the SAME row objects.
shallow = list(grid)
shallow[0][0] = 99                 # also changes grid[0][0]
print("after shallow[0][0] = 99, grid is: " + show(grid))

# Deep: copy every row too, so nothing is shared.
deep = [row[:] for row in grid]
deep[1][1] = -5                    # grid is not affected
print("after deep[1][1] = -5, grid is: " + show(grid))
print("the deep copy is: " + show(deep))
# Note: [[0] * 2] * 2 has the same trap: both rows are one shared list.
# Shallow copy: O(rows) time and space. Deep copy: O(rows * cols).

followUps:
Arrays.copyOf(grid, grid.length) makes a shallow copy: you get a new outer array, but each slot still points to the same row as the original.

Example: int[][] g = {{1, 2}, {3, 4}}; int[][] c = Arrays.copyOf(g, 2);. Now c[0][0] = 99 also changes g[0][0] to 99, because c[0] and g[0] are one row. But c[0] = new int[]{7, 7} does not affect g, because that only changes a slot in the new outer array.

If you ask for a longer length, the extra slots are null, not empty rows. For a deep copy, copy each row:

int[][] c = new int[g.length][];
for (int r = 0; r < g.length; r++)
  c[r] = Arrays.copyOf(g[r], g[r].length);

Shallow costs O(rows); deep costs O(rows × cols) time and space.

Walk the graph once and keep a map from each original node to its copy, so every node is cloned exactly once even when there are cycles.

  1. Create the copy of the start node and put it in the map.
  2. Do BFS or DFS. For each neighbour, create its copy if the map does not have it yet.
  3. Connect the copies by looking both ends up in the map.
Map<Node, Node> copy = new HashMap<>();
Node clone(Node u) {
  if (copy.containsKey(u)) return copy.get(u);
  Node c = new Node(u.val); copy.put(u, c);
  for (Node v : u.adj) c.adj.add(clone(v));
  return c;
}

The copy goes into the map before the neighbours are visited. In a cycle 1 → 2 → 1, when node 2 asks for node 1 it finds the copy already there instead of recursing forever. Time O(V + E), space O(V) for the map. For very deep graphs, use BFS with a queue to avoid deep recursion.

code.title: UTF-16 code units versus code points: reversing a string that contains an emoji
code.python:
def hex_cp(cp):
    return "U+" + format(cp, "X")


# 'a', one emoji (code point U+1F600), then 'b'.
s = "a\U0001F600b"
print("text: a, emoji U+1F600, b")

# Python strings count code points, so we encode to see what Java or JS would store.
raw = s.encode("utf-16-le")
units = [int.from_bytes(raw[i:i + 2], "little") for i in range(0, len(raw), 2)]
print("UTF-16 code units (length): " + str(len(units)))

cps = [ord(ch) for ch in s]            # real characters, one int each
print("code points: " + str(len(cps)))

# Correct reverse: walk the code points backwards.
print("reversed by code point: " + " ".join(hex_cp(c) for c in reversed(cps)))

# Wrong reverse: walking 16-bit units backwards splits the surrogate pair.
print("reversed by code unit (broken): " + " ".join(hex_cp(u) for u in reversed(units)))
# Time O(N), space O(N).

followUps:
Reverse it one code point at a time, not one char at a time, so the two halves of an emoji stay together and in the right order.

In Java the simplest correct way is new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString(): its reverse treats a surrogate pair as one unit. The manual way is:

int[] cp = s.codePoints().toArray();
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = cp.length - 1; i >= 0; i--)
  sb.appendCodePoint(cp[i]);

Example: "a", an emoji U+1F600, "b" is 4 chars: a, D83D, DE00, b. A char-by-char swap gives b, DE00, D83D, a, where the pair is backwards and shows as two broken symbols. By code point you get b, U+1F600, a.

One more level exists: flags, skin tones and family emoji are several code points shown as one picture. For those you must reverse by grapheme cluster, using java.text.BreakIterator. Time O(N), space O(N).

Because a String can never change after it is created, its hash code and its equality can never change while it sits in the map, so the map can always find it again.

Compare with a mutable key: put a List into a HashSet, then add an element to the list. Its hash changes, the set looks in a different bucket, and contains returns false although the object is inside.

Two more points help:

  • The hash is cached. A String computes its hash once (O(L) for L characters) and stores it in a field, so later lookups with the same object skip that work.
  • Equality is by content. Two separate String objects holding "cat" are equal and hash the same, which is what you want for keys.

Remember the cost is not truly O(1): a first lookup hashes L characters and a match compares up to L characters, so it is O(L) per operation.

code.title: Rolling array: LCS with the full table and with only two rows

followUps:
Roughly 200 MB in Java and about 360 MB in Python, compared with 40 MB for a plain int[] of the same length. The extra comes from storing each number as its own object plus a pointer to it.

StructurePer element107 elements
Java int[]4 bytes40 MB
Java ArrayList<Integer>4 (reference) + 16 (object)about 200 MB
Python list of int8 (pointer) + 28 (object)about 360 MB

These are typical 64-bit figures; small values are cheaper because Java shares −128 to 127 and Python shares −5 to 256. Growth of the backing array can add up to 50% on top for a moment.

So with a 256 MB limit, use int[] in Java, and array('i') or a NumPy array in Python, both 4 bytes per element.

Keep only two rows of the table, the previous one and the current one, because each LCS cell reads just three neighbours: left, up, and up-left.

int[] prev = new int[m + 1], cur = new int[m + 1];
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
  for (int j = 1; j <= m; j++)
    cur[j] = a[i-1] == b[j-1] ? prev[j-1] + 1 : Math.max(prev[j], cur[j-1]);
  int[] t = prev; prev = cur; cur = t;
}
return prev[m];

Here prev[j] is "up", prev[j-1] is "up-left" and cur[j-1] is "left". After a row is finished the two arrays swap roles, so nothing is copied. Column 0 of both rows stays 0, which is the base case.

For two strings of length 104, the full table is 108 ints = 400 MB, while two rows are about 80 KB. Time stays O(N × M). The price: you get only the length, and can no longer walk back through the table to print the subsequence itself.
